Projects and identity

A thinking space belongs to a project, and a project is one repository (or one subtree of one). For your spaces to still be there tomorrow, Tandem has to be able to look at a repository and know which project it is. That link is the card.

What a card is

A card holds a project’s minted id, its label, its product grouping, and enough to find the repository again. You never write one by hand — it is minted once, when you enable a project.

The id is minted at that moment and never changes. The label is yours and you can rename it whenever you like; renaming never moves the spaces, because nothing is keyed by the name. Enabling the same repository twice is refused: identity is immutable, and a second card would split one project’s history in two.

Where the card lives, and why

The card is kept in the store, at cards/<id>.yaml — beside the spaces filed under it, not inside your repository.

It used to live in the repository, at .tandem/space.yaml. That was wrong in a way that only showed up at the worst moment. The file was untracked, so it never travelled with a clone, and committing it would have put your private grouping and labels into a product’s source. Worse: restore a machine and the store came back whole — every space, every delivery, every record — while every repository on the new machine was a stranger to it. Nothing was deleted. It was unreachable, which to a person is the same thing.

Keeping the card in the store fixes that, because the store is the thing that gets backed up and restored.

How a repository is matched back to its card

From what the repository itself can always say about itself:

  • its git remote, and

  • the path of the project inside it (empty for a whole repository, or something like packages/web for a subtree).

So a fresh clone — new machine, different directory, different everything — re-attaches itself to its own spaces on sight. The remote is compared by what it points at, not by how it is spelled: git@github.com:you/thing.git and https://github.com/you/thing are one repository.

A repository with no remote at all is matched by where it sits on disk, and re-links itself if you move it.

Worktrees are not projects

A git worktree — a second checkout of a repository you already have — is a temporary view, not a project. It reports the same remote and the same path as the repository it came from, so a naive match would show one project once per open worktree. Tandem tells them apart and gives a worktree no identity of its own; enabling one is refused, and points you at the repository it belongs to.

.tandem/ in your repository

A card left by an older version is imported into the store the first time that project is seen, and then removed from the working tree. You do not have to do anything.

The .tandem/ directory itself stays, because it holds things that really are the repository’s own and belong with the source:

setup.json

the four facts the door proved about this repository — how to install it, how to prepare it, how to run one test, how to build it.

conventions.json

the repository’s own conventions, when it declares any.

prompts/

your per-repository prompt overrides.

Those are facts about the code, not about your grouping — so they stay with the code.
